titre: Two Latin Words That Force You to Show the Prisoner
accroche: An English law of 1679 does not say who may be imprisoned. It only obliges the jailer to produce the detainee and say why.
contenu_vulgarise:
Habeas corpus. The two words are the opening of a Latin formula by which a judge orders: that you have the body. The body of the detained person, brought before him, along with a statement of the reason for the detention.

The procedure existed in England well before 1679, but it worked poorly, for very concrete reasons. The jailer could be slow to respond. He could move the prisoner from one prison to another so that the order never reached the right place, or send him out of the kingdom, where the English judge had no power. The right existed; its exercise did not.

## A law concerned only with deadlines and penalties

The Habeas Corpus Act receives royal assent on May 27, 1679. What it brings is almost entirely procedural, and that is what makes it interesting. It sets deadlines within which the detainee must be produced before the court, and geographic rules. It forbids the jailer to transfer a prisoner from one prison to another or out of the country to evade the order. And it attaches heavy fines to these obligations, payable not to the Treasury but to the prisoner himself.

This last point deserves a pause. By making the detainee the beneficiary of the fine, the law gives him a personal interest in pursuing the matter, and turns a rule that the state ought to enforce into a rule that the victim has the means to enforce. It does not count on the virtue of public officials; it makes their disobedience costly and their victim able to profit from it.

The text itself passed by a narrow margin. Introduced in the Commons, amended by the Lords, it was adopted in haste because Charles II was ending the parliamentary session and the matter had to be finished.

## What a purely formal guarantee guarantees

The Habeas Corpus Act says nothing about what justifies a detention. It states no substantive right, limits no police power, defines no offense. One might think it weak for that reason. It is the opposite.

A substantive rule, one that says what is permitted, can be debated, interpreted, and made subject to exceptions, and its application depends on the good faith of whoever applies it. The obligation to produce a body before a judge, within a set time, on pain of a fine, cannot be debated. Either the person is there, or they are not.

That is why this procedure has survived three centuries and is found in the constitutions of a great many countries. It rests on the observation that arbitrary powers almost never operate by claiming arbitrariness: they operate in the shadows, through delay, through transfer, through silence. Compelling them to show is often enough to prevent.

repere.texte: The Habeas Corpus Act receives royal assent on May 27, 1679. The fines incurred by a jailer who disobeys are payable to the prisoner himself, not to the Treasury.
repere.source: Habeas Corpus Act 1679 (31 Cha. 2. c. 2), United Kingdom

carte.punch: The law does not say who may be detained. It only requires that he be shown, and quickly.
carte.idee: England's Habeas Corpus Act of 1679 states no substantive right. It sets deadlines for producing the detainee before a judge, forbids moving him to evade the order, and provides fines payable to the prisoner himself. A purely procedural guarantee, and that is its strength.

quiz.question: Why does the Habeas Corpus Act of 1679 have the fines incurred by the jailer paid to the prisoner himself?
choix: To compensate the detainee for the harm suffered during the days of irregular detention
Because the royal Treasury refused to collect sums arising from faults committed by its own agents
To prevent the Crown from profiting financially from irregularities committed in its prisons
To give the detainee a personal interest in pursuing the matter, instead of relying on the diligence of public officials
quiz.explication: By making the prisoner the beneficiary of the fine, the law turns an obligation the state ought to see respected into one the victim has both the means and the interest to enforce himself.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Before the 1679 law, how did a jailer concretely manage to keep the judge's order from taking effect?
choix: By arguing that the prisoner had already appeared before another judge
By moving the prisoner from one prison to another, or sending him out of the kingdom
By invoking a defect of form in the wording of the judge's order
By requiring the prisoner to pay the costs of his own appearance
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text recalls that before 1679, the jailer delayed his response or moved the prisoner, even out of the kingdom, so that the judge's order remained without effect.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How was the text of the Habeas Corpus Act adopted by the English Parliament?
choix: After several years of debate between the two houses of Parliament
By a unanimous vote of the Commons and the Lords sitting together
Introduced in the Commons, amended by the Lords, adopted in haste
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text was introduced in the Commons, amended by the Lords, then adopted in haste because Charles II was about to close the parliamentary session.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the order given by the judge in the habeas corpus procedure literally mean, according to the entry?
choix: That you have the body, that is, that the detainee be brought before the judge with the reason for his detention
That the truth be told, that is, that the jailer swear to the legality of the detention
That the body be freed, that is, that the prisoner leave prison immediately
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Latin formula, translated as “that you have the body,” orders only that the detainee be produced before the judge with the reason for his detention.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the entry, which of these statements about the Habeas Corpus Act of 1679 is accurate?
choix: It sets no deadline for producing the detainee before the court
It does not forbid the jailer to move the prisoner from one prison to another
It provides no fine in case the jailer disobeys
It says nothing about what justifies a detention, and defines no offense
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text is purely procedural: it sets deadlines and forbids transfers, but never says what makes a detention lawful nor defines any offense.
